---
title: Realtime
icon: Radio
description: Subscribe to live row changes over a WebSocket and react to inserts, updates and deletes as they happen.
---

import { Database, ShieldCheck, KeyRound } from 'lucide-react';

Realtime lets your app react to data as it changes instead of polling for it.
Open one WebSocket, subscribe to a table, and Applad pushes an event every time
a row is inserted, updated or deleted, so a chat updates, a dashboard ticks and
a list re-renders the moment the data behind it moves.

Under the hood Applad listens to PostgreSQL itself, so any write to a table
(from an SDK call, an API request, a function, or hand-written SQL) produces an
event. You do not publish events yourself; writing to a [database](/build/databases)
is what publishes them.

<Steps>
<Step>
### Connect

Open a single WebSocket with `client.realtime.connect()`. The SDK points it at
`/v1/realtime` on your API and reuses the same socket for every subscription.
</Step>
<Step>
### Subscribe

Pick a table and attach callbacks. In Dart the `.database(databaseId, tableName)`
builder does this; in JS you pass the channel string to `subscribe(channel, callback)`.
</Step>
<Step>
### React and tidy up

Handle inserts, updates and deletes as events arrive, then call the returned
handle to stop listening and `disconnect()` when you are done.
</Step>
</Steps>

## Connecting

Realtime is exposed on the client SDK as `client.realtime`. It connects to the
`/v1/realtime` WebSocket endpoint on your API, passing the project as a query
parameter.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
import { Applad } from '@mittolabs/applad';

const client = new Applad({
  endpoint: 'https://api.applad.io',
  projectId: 'your-project-id',
});

client.realtime.connect();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
import 'package:applad/applad.dart';

final client = Applad(
  endpoint: 'https://api.applad.io',
  projectId: 'your-project-id',
);

client.realtime.connect();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

The SDK rewrites the `http`/`https` endpoint to `ws`/`wss` for you, so the
socket opens at `wss://api.applad.io/v1/realtime?project=your-project-id`.
`connect()` is idempotent; calling it twice does nothing while a socket is
already open.

## Subscribing to table changes

The JS client subscribes to a channel directly and gives you the full event, so
you branch on `event.type` yourself. The Dart client exposes a fluent builder
for the common case: watch one table and attach a callback per event type. Each
callback receives the affected row as a plain map.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
const channel = `databases.${client.projectId}.app.messages`;

const unsubscribe = client.realtime.subscribe(channel, (event) => {
  const payload = event.payload as {
    action: string;
    new?: Record<string, unknown>;
    old?: Record<string, unknown>;
  };

  switch (event.type) {
    case 'databases.rows.create':
      console.log('new message', payload.new);
      break;
    case 'databases.rows.update':
      console.log('edited', payload.new);
      break;
    case 'databases.rows.delete':
      console.log('removed', payload.old);
      break;
  }
});
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
final sub = client.realtime
    .database('app', 'messages')      // databaseId, tableName
    .onInsert((row) => print('new message: ${row['body']}'))
    .onUpdate((row) => print('edited: ${row['body']}'))
    .onDelete((row) => print('removed: ${row['id']}'))
    .subscribe();
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

You do not have to handle every event type. Attach only the callbacks you care
about; the others are ignored.

## Channels

A subscription is scoped by a **channel** string. Table-level row changes use:

```
databases.<projectId>.<databaseId>.<tableName>
```

For example, `databases.proj_123.app.messages` is every row change in the
`messages` table of the `app` database. This is exactly the channel the Dart
`.database(databaseId, tableName)` builder computes for you, and the one you
pass by hand to `subscribe(channel, callback)` in JS.

<Callout title="Delivery is table-scoped, not permission-filtered">
Today, realtime delivers a table's changes to every subscriber on that table's
channel. It does **not** yet apply row-level [permissions](/build/permissions) to the
stream, so a subscriber receives events for rows it might not be allowed to read
through the REST API. Treat a channel as a broadcast within a table: only
subscribe from contexts allowed to see the whole table, and do not rely on
realtime to hide rows. This is a known limitation, tracked separately from the
permission checks enforced on reads and writes.
</Callout>

## The event payload

Every message the server sends has the same envelope:

| Field | Description |
| --- | --- |
| `type` | `databases.rows.create`, `databases.rows.update`, or `databases.rows.delete` |
| `channel` | the channel the event was published to |
| `timestamp` | RFC 3339 UTC time of the change |
| `payload` | the change itself (see below) |

The `payload` describes the row that changed:

```json
{
  "project_id": "proj_123",
  "database_id": "app",
  "schema": "p_proj_123_app",
  "table": "messages",
  "action": "insert",
  "old": null,
  "new": { "id": "m_9", "body": "hello", "created_at": "2026-07-28T12:00:00Z" },
  "timestamp": "2026-07-28T12:00:00Z"
}
```

- `new` holds the row after the change and is present for inserts and updates.
- `old` holds the row before the change and is present for updates and deletes.
- The row objects carry your table's real column names at the top level.

In Dart you rarely touch the payload directly. The builder callbacks already
hand you the right row: `onInsert`/`onUpdate` receive `new`, and `onDelete`
receives `old`. If you subscribe to a raw channel with
`client.realtime.subscribe`, the `RealtimeEvent` exposes `event.row` (the `new`
row, falling back to `old`) and `event.oldRow` (the `old` row) as convenience
getters.

## Unsubscribing and disconnecting

`subscribe()` returns a handle you use to stop listening. Cancelling one
subscription leaves the socket open for the others.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
unsubscribe();             // stop this subscription
client.realtime.disconnect();   // close the socket and clear listeners
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
sub.cancel();              // stop this subscription
client.realtime.disconnect();   // close the socket entirely
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

Always cancel a subscription when the view that owns it goes away (a disposed
widget, an unmounted component) so callbacks do not fire into dead state, and
call `disconnect()` when your app no longer needs realtime at all.

## A complete example

Connect, keep a local list in sync with a table, then tear everything down.

<Tabs items={['JavaScript', 'Dart']}>
<Tab value="JavaScript">
```ts
import { Applad } from '@mittolabs/applad';

const client = new Applad({
  endpoint: 'https://api.applad.io',
  projectId: 'your-project-id',
});

const messages: Record<string, unknown>[] = [];
client.realtime.connect();

const channel = `databases.${client.projectId}.app.messages`;
const unsubscribe = client.realtime.subscribe(channel, (event) => {
  const p = event.payload as {
    new?: Record<string, unknown>;
    old?: Record<string, unknown>;
  };
  if (event.type === 'databases.rows.create' && p.new) {
    messages.push(p.new);
  } else if (event.type === 'databases.rows.update' && p.new) {
    const i = messages.findIndex((m) => m.id === p.new!.id);
    if (i !== -1) messages[i] = p.new;
  } else if (event.type === 'databases.rows.delete' && p.old) {
    const i = messages.findIndex((m) => m.id === p.old!.id);
    if (i !== -1) messages.splice(i, 1);
  }
});

// When you are done:
unsubscribe();
client.realtime.disconnect();
```
</Tab>
<Tab value="Dart">
```dart
import 'package:applad/applad.dart';

Future<void> main() async {
  final client = Applad(
    endpoint: 'https://api.applad.io',
    projectId: 'your-project-id',
  );

  final messages = <Map<String, dynamic>>[];

  client.realtime.connect();

  final sub = client.realtime
      .database('app', 'messages')
      .onInsert((row) => messages.add(row))
      .onUpdate((row) {
        final i = messages.indexWhere((m) => m['id'] == row['id']);
        if (i != -1) messages[i] = row;
      })
      .onDelete((row) => messages.removeWhere((m) => m['id'] == row['id']))
      .subscribe();

  // ... run your app; events arrive as rows change ...

  // When you are done:
  sub.cancel();
  client.realtime.disconnect();
}
```
</Tab>
</Tabs>

## Notes for self-hosting

Realtime needs the PostgreSQL change-capture trigger, which ships in the initial
migration and is installed automatically, so no extra setup is required for a
single instance. If you run more than one API instance behind a load balancer,
set `REDIS_ADDR` (Redis is already part of the default stack) so events fan out
across instances: without it, a client connected to one instance only sees
changes that instance observed. The WebSocket rides the same `/v1` origin as the
rest of the API, so the Caddy edge proxies it with no special configuration.
